claims.text: The initial sub-10 nm Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles are equiatomic single-phase solid solutions.
The sluggish-diffusion assumption breaks down above 700 K in sub-10 nm Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles.
Thermal exposure can destabilize a nominally single-phase high-entropy alloy and cause precipitation or phase separation.
In these nanoparticles, surface-energy minimization dominates configurational-entropy stabilization at elevated temperature.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of sub-10 nm particles makes surface-energy terms dominant.
Surface diffusion coefficients in the nanoparticles are enhanced relative to bulk diffusion coefficients.
Above 700 K, the driving force for reducing total surface energy overcomes the kinetic barrier associated with sluggish bulk diffusion.
Au and Cu are the lower-surface-energy elements in this alloy and therefore segregate to particle surfaces.
Loss of configurational entropy in the particle core drives phase separation.
High particle curvature creates a chemical-potential gradient that accelerates Ostwald ripening.
Ostwald ripening causes smaller particles to dissolve and feed larger particles.
Heating will rapidly remove particles smaller than 5 nm through dissolution and coalescence.
Heating will produce an Au/Cu-enriched surface or core-shell structure.
Surface-energy minimization will drive a transition from spherical particles to faceted or anisotropic shapes.
Surface diffusion will dominate to such an extent that the bulk sluggish-diffusion effect is negligible.
High configurational entropy and sluggish atomic diffusion can suppress precipitation and stabilize single-phase high-entropy alloys.
Kinetic limitations can cause experiments to depart from thermodynamic-equilibrium predictions in high-entropy alloys.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to sub-10 nm particles and may not apply to particles larger than 50 nm or to bulk material.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and mechanism specify a breakdown threshold above 700 K, while the uncertainty field states that the exact threshold for this five-component system is unknown. Moreover, the nearest cited thermal evidence concerns 700 °C (approximately 973 K), not 700 K.
